title: Anthropic says Claude designed working protein binders for 14 of 15 targets
subtitle: Independent labs at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience validated Claude-designed binders at a 22–35 percent hit rate, roughly double the field's typical 10–15 percent.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic published lab-validated results this week showing that its Claude Opus 4.8 and Mythos Preview models designed de novo protein binders — small proteins engineered to stick to a target — that succeeded against 14 of 15 targets in blind wet-lab tests. The models generated 30 candidate binders per target, producing 1,320 designs in total. Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience independently manufactured and screened the sequences, and 354 designs bound to their intended targets across the exercise. Against one particularly hard target, RBX1, Mythos Preview hit 40 percent versus 3.7 percent among human participants in a public design competition.

The result matters because it is the first rigorous, third-party validation of a general-purpose LLM performing at or above the level of specialized protein-design pipelines. Anthropic reports a 35.1 percent overall hit rate for Mythos Preview when each target is handled independently — roughly double the 10 to 15 percent hit rate typical of current protein-design campaigns. The models were not fine-tuned on protein data. They reasoned through the design problem the way they would any other complex task, using the same general capabilities that drive coding and math benchmarks.

Google DeepMind's AlphaFold and RFdiffusion have dominated computational protein design for the last five years, and both use architectures purpose-built for structural biology. A general-purpose LLM matching or beating that class of tool suggests the one-model-many-domains thesis is stronger than critics have allowed. Anthropic is careful to note the limit: protein binders are not drugs. Getting a molecule to stick to a target is the first step of a multi-year pipeline that also has to clear stability, toxicity, and manufacturability hurdles.

For learners: this is worth reading in the primary source, not the summary. Anthropic's paper describes the exact prompts, the target list, and the way the model was allowed to iterate. The interesting question is not whether Claude can design proteins — that is settled — but which parts of the workflow the model handled and which parts the human researchers still shaped. That boundary is the shape of AI-for-science work for the next few years.
